```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 3.5)
# Steps 4 to 9 need TRAMO (package RJDemetra, which needs Java). Their
# output was computed by data-raw/oecd_idn_vignette.R with the code shown
# below and is read from inst/vignette-results/.
vr <- readRDS(system.file("vignette-results", "oecd-indonesia.rds",
                          package = "cyclind"))
va <- vr$part_a
vb <- vr$part_b
r2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
num <- function(x) format(x, trim = TRUE)
cap <- function(s) paste0(toupper(substr(s, 1, 1)), substring(s, 2))
label <- c(share_prices = "share prices",
           call_money_rate = "the call-money rate",
           rupiah_per_usd = "the exchange rate",
           consumer_confidence = "consumer confidence")
words <- function(x) {
  x <- unname(label[x])
  if (length(x) < 2) return(x)
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
}
failing <- function(assess, reason) {
  assess$name[grepl(reason, assess$reasons, fixed = TRUE)]
}
words_num <- function(x) {
  x <- num(x)
  if (length(x) < 2) return(x)
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
}
agree <- function(v, stat) v$agreement$x[v$agreement$statistic == stat]
```

The OECD publishes a composite leading indicator (CLI) for Indonesia,
together with its reference series (monthly GDP) and its seven
components. For four components the OECD also publishes the original
series: share prices, the call-money rate, the rupiah exchange rate and
consumer confidence. cyclind ships these series, downloaded from the OECD
Data Explorer on 13 November 2026, in `inst/extdata/oecd-idn/`, one CSV
file per indicator. This vignette builds a CLI from them with
`oecd_spec()`, twice: first against the growth cycle of GDP (the deviation
from its trend, the OECD's own reference), then against the growth rate
cycle of GDP (its annual growth rate). The last section repeats the steps
in the graphical interface.

Steps 1 to 3 run when the vignette is built. Steps 4 to 9 need the TRAMO
program of JDemetra+ (package **RJDemetra**, which needs Java) for the
outliers, the log/level test and the forecasts that extend each series.
To keep the vignette free of Java, their output was computed with the
code shown here by `data-raw/oecd_idn_vignette.R` and is printed from
`inst/vignette-results/oecd-indonesia.rds`; the provenance of that
computation is at the end. The code runs as shown when RJDemetra is
installed.

# Part A. Reference: the growth cycle of GDP

## Step 1. Data

```{r data}
library(cyclind)
dir <- system.file("extdata", "oecd-idn", package = "cyclind")
files <- file.path(dir, c("gdp.csv", "share_prices.csv",
                          "call_money_rate.csv", "rupiah_per_usd.csv",
                          "consumer_confidence.csv"))
series <- read_cli_series(files)
vapply(series, attr, "", "frequency")
oecd <- read_cli_data(file.path(dir, "oecd_cli.csv"))
```

GDP is quarterly and the candidates are monthly. `cli_align()` brings GDP
to months with the Denton-Cholette method, which keeps the quarterly
totals. The OECD derives its monthly GDP reference with a method of its
own, which cyclind does not reproduce. The interest rate is a monthly
average.

```{r align}
x <- cli_align(series, type = c(gdp = "flow", call_money_rate = "average"),
               reference = "gdp")
attr(x, "alignment")
```

## Step 2. Candidates and their economic rationale

The OECD requires an economic rationale for each component and sets its
direction from it. Share prices and consumer confidence are
procyclical; a higher interest rate and a weaker rupiah (more rupiah per
dollar) come before slower growth, so both are inverted.

```{r candidates}
meta <- data.frame(
  name = c("share_prices", "call_money_rate", "rupiah_per_usd",
           "consumer_confidence"),
  rationale = c("expectations", "prime_mover", "prime_mover",
                "expectations"),
  sign = c(1, -1, -1, 1))
cand <- cli_candidates(x, reference = "gdp", meta = meta)
cand
```

## Step 3. The OECD specification

`oecd_spec()` follows the OECD documents where they state a rule (Gyomai
and Guidetti 2012; Gyomai, Ahmad and Astolfi 2017): TRAMO-type outliers,
of which only additive outliers are removed (`outlier_types = "AO"`), two
months of forecasts, the log/level test, the double Hodrick-Prescott
filter (12 to 120 months), Bry-Boschan turning points with phases of at
least 9 and cycles of at least 24 months, a matching window of 24 months
lead and 9 months lag, the median-lead classification with cyclical
conformity, and no lag-shifting. Where the documents give no formula, it
takes the choices that come closest to the published CLI of Indonesia:
chained average log growth with counter-cyclical components entering as
reciprocals, and an amplitude matched by standard deviations. The section
"The OECD method and the defaults" of `vignette("cyclind")` shows how
close these choices come when the seven component cycles published by the
OECD are aggregated; `?oecd_spec` gives the source of each step.

```{r spec}
spec <- oecd_spec(engine = "tramo")
spec
```

`engine = "tramo"` asks for TRAMO, as the OECD uses. The default,
`"auto"`, takes TRAMO when RJDemetra is installed and the regARIMA part of
X-13ARIMA-SEATS (package **seasonal**) otherwise. X-13 is a different
program: it finds other outliers, so its results differ from those shown
here.

## Step 4. Cycles

```{r cycles, eval = FALSE}
cyc <- cli_cycles(cand, spec)
cyc$gdp@steps
```

```{r cycles-out, echo = FALSE}
va$steps
```

Every outlier treatment reports what it found. `outlier_report()` lists
the outliers that were removed and, in brackets in its column `periods`,
those that were detected but kept:

```{r outliers, eval = FALSE}
outlier_report(cyc)[, c("name", "n_removed", "n_kept", "types")]
```

```{r outliers-out, echo = FALSE}
va$outliers[, c("name", "n_removed", "n_kept", "types")]
```

Following the OECD documentation of 2017, only the
`r sum(va$outliers$n_removed)` additive outliers are replaced; the
`r sum(va$outliers$n_kept)` transitory changes and level shifts are
reported but stay in the series.

The OECD's own reference cycle is in `oecd_cli.csv`. The GDP cycle that
cyclind extracts from quarterly GDP follows it closely:

```{r reference, eval = FALSE}
ref <- stats::ts.intersect(cyclind = cyc$gdp@normalised,
                           oecd = oecd[, "reference_normalised"])
cor(ref[stats::complete.cases(ref), ])[1, 2]
```

```{r reference-out, echo = FALSE}
va$cor_reference
```

## Step 5. Turning points

```{r turning-points, eval = FALSE}
tps <- cli_turning_points(cyc, spec)
as.data.frame(tps$gdp)[, c("period", "type")]
```

```{r turning-points-out, echo = FALSE}
va$tps
```

## Step 6. Classification

```{r assess, eval = FALSE}
a <- cli_assess(cand, spec, cyc)
as.data.frame(a)[, c("name", "class", "median_lead", "n_matched",
                     "extra", "reasons")]
```

```{r assess-out, echo = FALSE}
va$assess
```

No candidate passes the OECD rule with cyclical conformity. All four lead
GDP by their median lead (`r num(min(va$assess$median_lead))` to
`r num(max(va$assess$median_lead))` months), but
`r words(failing(va$assess, "extra"))` have too many extra turning points,
and `r words(failing(va$assess, "concordance"))` fail the concordance
test.

## Step 7. Composite

`cli_build()` keeps the leading candidates and chains their average
growth; like the OECD in practice, `oecd_spec()` does not shift them by
their leads. Because no candidate leads, `cli_build()` builds no
composite and says so; the composite of the four components is built with
`cli_composite()` from the inverted cycles that `cli_build()` returns.

```{r build, eval = FALSE}
res <- cli_build(cand, spec)
leaders(res)
cy <- cycles(res)
cli4 <- cli_composite(cy, meta$name, spec, cy$gdp)
cli4
both <- stats::ts.intersect(cyclind = cli4@cycle,
                            oecd = oecd[, "cli_normalised"])
cor(both[stats::complete.cases(both), ])[1, 2]
```

```{r build-out, echo = FALSE}
message(paste("Warning:", va$build_warnings))
va$leaders
writeLines(va$cli4)
va$cor_oecd
```

The OECD CLI uses seven components, three of which (producer prices,
production of non-metallic products and tourism) are not published as
original series, so the composite of four follows it only roughly. A
crisis can dominate a correlation on its own; `cycle_agreement()`
measures the agreement without 2020 and 2021 and gives block-bootstrap
intervals from an explicit `seed`:

```{r agreement, eval = FALSE}
cycle_agreement(cli4, oecd[, "cli_normalised"],
                exclude = c(2020, 2021 + 11 / 12), reps = 499, seed = 1)
```

```{r agreement-out, echo = FALSE}
va$agreement
```

Without the two crisis years the Pearson correlation is
`r r2(agree(va, "pearson"))` and the rank correlation
`r r2(agree(va, "spearman"))`.

## Step 8. Validation

`cli_validate()` and `cli_quality()` judge the composite against the GDP
cycle:

```{r validate, eval = FALSE}
val <- cli_validate(cli4, cy$gdp, spec)
cli_quality(val, spec)
```

```{r validate-out, echo = FALSE}
writeLines(va$quality)
```

The composite leads the turning points of GDP, but its probabilities of
contraction do not beat the naive forecast, so the verdict is
*`r va$quality_verdict`*.

## Step 9. Presentation

The three OECD forms: the amplitude-adjusted CLI, the trend-restored CLI
and its 12-month rate of change. The trend-restored CLI is left missing
after the last observation of GDP, as the OECD does.

```{r presentation, eval = FALSE}
pres <- cli_presentation(res, cli4)
tail(pres[, c("time", "amplitude_adjusted", "trend_restored",
              "rate_of_change")])
```

```{r presentation-out, echo = FALSE}
tail(va$presentation[, c("time", "amplitude_adjusted", "trend_restored",
                         "rate_of_change")])
```

```{r plot-data, eval = FALSE}
idx <- cli4@index
```

```{r plot-data-stored, include = FALSE}
idx <- va$index
```

```{r plot, fig.alt = "CLI of four components and the OECD CLI, 1997-2026"}
a2 <- stats::ts.intersect(cyclind = idx,
                          oecd = oecd[, "cli_amplitude_adjusted"])
ok <- stats::time(a2)[stats::complete.cases(a2)]
a2 <- stats::window(a2, start = min(ok), end = max(ok))
plot(a2[, "cyclind"], ylab = "Index (trend = 100)", xlab = NULL,
     ylim = range(a2, na.rm = TRUE),
     main = "CLI of four components (cyclind) and the OECD CLI")
lines(a2[, "oecd"], col = "grey50")
abline(h = 100, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("cyclind, four components", "OECD, seven components"),
       col = c("black", "grey50"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

# Part B. Reference: the growth rate cycle of GDP

Users often follow the growth rate of GDP rather than its deviation from
trend. The OECD serves them with the 12-month rate of change of its
trend-restored CLI (`cli_growth_rate` in `oecd_cli.csv`; Gyomai and
Guidetti 2012, p. 11). In cyclind the reference itself can be a growth
rate: the cycle form `growth_form()` turns every series into its annual
growth rate, `100 * (Y_t / Y_{t-12} - 1)`, after the outlier treatment,
and a Hodrick-Prescott smoother (no detrending) then removes the short
movements. The call-money rate, a percentage, is given `unit = "percent"`
so that its change is a difference in percentage points. The form is
experimental: the OECD thresholds were set for growth cycles. Step 1 is
the same as in Part A.

## Step 2. Candidates, with the unit of the interest rate

```{r candidates-growth}
meta_g <- meta
meta_g$unit <- c(NA, "percent", NA, NA)
cand_g <- cli_candidates(x, reference = "gdp", meta = meta_g)
```

## Step 3. The OECD specification with the growth rate form

```{r spec-growth}
spec_g <- oecd_spec(engine = "tramo", form = growth_form())
spec_g
```

## Step 4. Cycles

```{r cycles-growth, eval = FALSE}
cyc_g <- cli_cycles(cand_g, spec_g)
cyc_g$gdp@steps
```

```{r cycles-growth-out, echo = FALSE}
vb$steps
```

The growth rate cycle of GDP moves with the 12-month rate of change of
the OECD CLI, which leads it by a few months:

```{r reference-growth, eval = FALSE}
gy <- oecd[, "cli_growth_rate"]
lead_cor <- function(k) {
  z <- stats::ts.intersect(stats::lag(gy, -k), cyc_g$gdp@cycle)
  cor(z[stats::complete.cases(z), ])[1, 2]
}
sapply(c(lead_0 = 0, lead_3 = 3, lead_6 = 6), lead_cor)
```

```{r reference-growth-out, echo = FALSE}
gy <- oecd[, "cli_growth_rate"]
vb$lead_cor
```

## Step 5. Turning points

The growth rate cycle has `r nrow(vb$tps)` turning points, the growth
cycle of Part A `r nrow(va$tps)`:

```{r turning-points-growth, eval = FALSE}
tps_g <- cli_turning_points(cyc_g, spec_g)
as.data.frame(tps_g$gdp)[, c("period", "type")]
```

```{r turning-points-growth-out, echo = FALSE}
vb$tps
```

## Step 6. Classification

```{r assess-growth, eval = FALSE}
a_g <- cli_assess(cand_g, spec_g, cyc_g)
as.data.frame(a_g)[, c("name", "class", "median_lead", "n_matched",
                       "extra", "reasons")]
```

```{r assess-growth-out, echo = FALSE}
vb$assess
```

```{r growth-numbers, include = FALSE}
lead_b <- vb$assess[vb$assess$class == "leading", ]
fail_b <- vb$assess[grepl("concordance", vb$assess$reasons), ]
```

Only `r words(lead_b$name)` pass, with a median lead of
`r num(lead_b$median_lead)` months. `r cap(words(fail_b$name))` lead by
`r words_num(fail_b$median_lead)` months
respectively, but their phases do not agree with those of GDP growth
often enough for the concordance test.

## Step 7. Composite

`cli_build()` keeps `r words(vb$leaders)` alone and warns that a
composite of fewer than three components is little more than the cycle of
its components; to compare with the OECD, the composite of the four growth
rates is again built with `cli_composite()`.

```{r build-growth, eval = FALSE}
res_g <- cli_build(cand_g, spec_g)
leaders(res_g)
cy_g <- cycles(res_g)
cli4_g <- cli_composite(cy_g, meta$name, spec_g, cy_g$gdp)
cli4_g
both_g <- stats::ts.intersect(cyclind = cli4_g@cycle, oecd = gy)
cor(both_g[stats::complete.cases(both_g), ])[1, 2]
cycle_agreement(cli4_g, gy, exclude = c(2020, 2021 + 11 / 12),
                reps = 499, seed = 1)
```

```{r build-growth-out, echo = FALSE}
message(paste("Warning:", vb$build_warnings))
vb$leaders
writeLines(vb$cli4)
vb$cor_oecd
vb$agreement
```

The composite of the four growth rates correlates
`r r2(vb$cor_oecd)` with the 12-month rate of change of the OECD CLI
(`r r2(agree(vb, "pearson"))` without 2020 and 2021), although it is
built from four of the seven components.

## Step 8. Validation

```{r validate-growth, eval = FALSE}
val_g <- cli_validate(cli4_g, cy_g$gdp, spec_g)
cli_quality(val_g, spec_g)
```

```{r validate-growth-out, echo = FALSE}
writeLines(vb$quality)
```

The composite leads the turning points of GDP growth, but its
probabilities of a downturn do worse than the naive forecast: the leads
are too irregular to time slowdowns.

## Step 9. Presentation

With the growth rate form, the trend-restored series is a growth rate in
percent (the cycle plus the mean growth of GDP), and a 12-month rate of
change of a growth rate has no meaning, so it is left empty. The plot
standardises both series to compare their timing on one axis.

```{r presentation-growth, eval = FALSE}
pres_g <- cli_presentation(res_g, cli4_g)
tail(pres_g[, c("time", "amplitude_adjusted", "trend_restored")])
```

```{r presentation-growth-out, echo = FALSE}
tail(vb$presentation[, c("time", "amplitude_adjusted", "trend_restored")])
```

```{r plot-growth-data, eval = FALSE}
cyc4_g <- cli4_g@cycle
```

```{r plot-growth-data-stored, include = FALSE}
cyc4_g <- vb$cycle
```

```{r plot-growth, fig.alt = "Standardised growth rate cycles, 1998-2026"}
std <- function(z) (z - mean(z, na.rm = TRUE)) / stats::sd(z, na.rm = TRUE)
g2 <- stats::ts.intersect(cyclind = cyc4_g, oecd = gy)
ok <- stats::time(g2)[stats::complete.cases(g2)]
g2 <- stats::window(g2, start = min(ok), end = max(ok))
s2 <- stats::ts(apply(g2, 2, std), start = stats::start(g2),
                frequency = stats::frequency(g2))
plot(s2[, "cyclind"], ylab = "Standardised", xlab = NULL,
     ylim = range(s2, na.rm = TRUE),
     main = "Growth rate cycle: cyclind composite and the OECD CLI")
lines(s2[, "oecd"], col = "grey50")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("cyclind, four components",
                        "OECD CLI, 12-month rate of change"),
       col = c("black", "grey50"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

# The same in the graphical interface

`run_app()` opens the interface (it needs the shiny package). English is
the default; `run_app(language = "id")` gives the same interface in
Indonesian. The files are in the folder printed by
`system.file("extdata", "oecd-idn", package = "cyclind")`.

1. **Data.** Source *Upload several files (one per indicator)*; select
   `gdp.csv`, `share_prices.csv`, `call_money_rate.csv`,
   `rupiah_per_usd.csv` and `consumer_confidence.csv`; analysis frequency
   *Monthly*; variable type of the reference series *Flow*.
2. **Candidate metadata.** Reference series `gdp`. For each candidate set
   the rationale and the direction as in step 2 (the interest rate and the
   exchange rate countercyclical) and the variable type of the interest
   rate *Average*. For Part B also set the unit of the interest rate to
   *Ratio/percent*.
3. **Specification.** Method *OECD method, with notes*. The interface uses
   `oecd_spec()`. Set *Engine of the TRAMO outliers* to *TRAMO (package
   RJDemetra)*, as in this vignette; the automatic choice takes TRAMO when
   RJDemetra is installed and X-13 otherwise. For Part B set *Cycle form*
   to *Growth rate cycle: growth rate* and *Growth rate period* to
   *Annual (y-on-y)*.
4. Steps 4 to 8 of the interface run the cycles, turning points,
   classification, composite and validation. Automatic mode finds no
   leader in Part A and keeps `r words(vb$leaders)` in Part B; choose the
   four components by hand for the composites above. The OECD method does
   not shift the components by their leads, so the composite of the
   interface equals `cli_composite(cy, meta$name, spec, cy$gdp)` of this
   vignette.
5. Step 9 builds a composite coincident index, which this vignette does
   not need. Step 10 downloads the results, the OECD forms of
   presentation of step 9 above and an R script that reproduces them with
   the same functions as this vignette and prints their provenance
   (`cyclind_provenance()`, as below).

# Provenance of the stored results

`cyclind_provenance()` records the versions of the software and the MD5
checksums of the data. The results of steps 4 to 9 were computed on
`r vr$created` with:

```{r provenance, echo = FALSE}
vr$provenance
```

# References

Gyomai, G., Ahmad, N. and Astolfi, R. (2017). The OECD system of composite
leading indicators. In G. L. Mazzi and A. Ozyildirim (eds.), *Handbook on
Cyclical Composite Indicators for Business Cycle Analysis*, chapter 10,
273–291. Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg.
<https://doi.org/10.2785/962890>

Gyomai, G. and Guidetti, E. (2012). *OECD System of Composite Leading
Indicators*. OECD, Paris.
<https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/data/methods/OECD-System-of-Composite-Leading-Indicators.pdf>
